title: SIX CITIES FOR ONE DESPERATE SOUL: THE DAY GOD MADE A WAY FOR THE PERSON EVERYONE WANTED TO KILL
paragraphs: SIX CITIES FOR ONE DESPERATE SOUL: THE DAY GOD MADE A WAY FOR THE PERSON EVERYONE WANTED TO KILL

Why did God command Joshua to establish six cities of refuge? The forgotten story in Joshua 20:1–9 reveals something breathtaking about justice, mercy, guilt, and the Savior who became our refuge when there was nowhere else to run.
Imagine running for your life.
Your lungs are burning. Your legs are shaking. Your heartbeat is louder than your footsteps.
Behind you is someone who wants you dead.
And the most terrifying part?
You cannot say that nothing happened.
Someone is dead.
You were involved.
There is blood on the ground, a grieving family, and a terrible moment you would give anything to undo.
You did not plan it. You did not wake up that morning intending to destroy a life. But something happened, and now nothing will ever be the same.
You cannot rewind the moment.
You cannot resurrect the person.
You cannot convince the grieving family that their pain is less real simply because your intentions were different.
So you run.
Not because you are innocent of everything.
But because you are not guilty of what everyone thinks you did.
And somewhere ahead, beyond the dust and the hills, stands a city.
A city God Himself commanded to exist.
A city where your story might not end in death.
Now imagine reaching its gates, collapsing before the elders, and trying to explain through tears what happened.
Will they listen?
Will they turn you away?
Will they protect you until the truth is established?
This is not a scene from a Hollywood thriller.
This is the world behind Joshua chapter 20.
And hidden inside these nine verses is one of the most extraordinary revelations of God's justice and mercy in the Old Testament.
Because long before Jesus walked toward Calvary, God was already teaching His people something the human heart desperately needed to understand.
Mercy is not the absence of justice. And justice, in the hands of a holy God, does not have to become revenge.
But there is something even deeper here.
Something that reaches beyond ancient Israel.
Beyond the six cities.
Beyond the blood avenger.
Something that reaches the person reading this article right now who has been carrying a mistake, a regret, a secret, or a shame they cannot seem to outrun.
Stay with me.
Because before this story is over, you may discover that the most important question is not how far you have fallen.
It is where you are running.
The Israelites had finally entered the land God promised their ancestors.
The wilderness years were behind them. Joshua had led them through battles, victories, setbacks, and the division of the land among the tribes.
But God was not finished establishing how His people should live.
He was concerned with more than territory.
More than borders.
More than military victories.
He was establishing a community in which human life mattered, justice had boundaries, and the vulnerable were not automatically abandoned to the anger of the powerful.
Then the LORD spoke to Joshua.
Joshua 20:2 records the command:
"Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses." (KJV)
The instruction was not a sudden new idea.
God had already spoken through Moses about cities of refuge in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19.
Joshua was now commanded to put those instructions into practice.
And the reason was astonishingly specific.
Joshua 20:3 says:
"That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood." (KJV)
Notice those words.
"Unawares and unwittingly."
This was not a sanctuary for someone who deliberately murdered another human being and simply wanted to escape the consequences.
God was not commanding Israel to protect calculated violence.
He was distinguishing between intentional murder and an unintentional killing.
That distinction mattered.
It still matters.
Because God does not treat every tragic outcome as though every human intention behind it were identical.
Consider the example given in Deuteronomy 19:5.
Two men go into the forest to cut wood.
One swings an axe.
The iron head slips from the handle, strikes his companion, and kills him.
There was no hatred.
No premeditation.
No ambush.
Yet a man is dead.
A family is grieving.
And the surviving man is facing a danger that could turn one tragedy into another.
In ancient Israel, a close relative of the deceased could act as the avenger of blood.
The Hebrew expression is גֹּאֵל הַדָּם (go'el ha-dam).
The word go'el refers to a family redeemer or one who acts on behalf of a relative. Dam means blood.
In this legal setting, the expression describes the blood avenger.
The role existed within Israel's ancient kinship and justice system, but God placed restrictions on how that role could operate.
Grief did not grant unlimited authority.
Anger did not establish guilt.
And revenge was not allowed to replace a proper judgment.
Think about that.
God knew how quickly wounded people could become dangerous people.
He knew that a grieving relative might act before the facts were established.
He knew that emotion, however understandable, could produce another irreversible death.
So He established a place where an accused person could reach safety and receive a hearing.
Not because the death of the victim did not matter.
But precisely because human life mattered so much that another life must not be taken unjustly.
And here is where the original Hebrew opens another window into the passage.
The expression translated "cities of refuge" is עָרֵי מִקְלָט (arei miqlat).
Arei means "cities of," and miqlat means "refuge" or "asylum."
These were designated places of protection.
Not places where truth disappeared.
Not places where accountability was abolished.
But places where a person could be sheltered from immediate retaliation while the matter was judged.
The Hebrew description of the killing also matters.
Joshua 20:3 uses בִּשְׁגָגָה (bishgagah), meaning "unintentionally" or "inadvertently," together with בִּבְלִי־דַעַת (bivli-da'at), meaning "without knowledge."
The emphasis is not on pretending that a death never occurred.
It is on recognizing that intention and knowledge are morally and legally significant.
God's justice was not blind rage.
And His mercy was not careless permission.
Both were operating together.
That should make us stop and examine our own hearts.
How many relationships have been destroyed because someone heard one accusation and never asked another question?
How many people have been condemned by rumors before they were given an opportunity to speak?
How many families have suffered because anger was allowed to make decisions that wisdom should have made?
And how often have we wanted God to understand our intentions while refusing to consider the intentions of someone who hurt us?
That question is uncomfortable.
But sometimes the Word of God must expose what we would rather excuse.
The cities of refuge remind us that the truth matters even when emotions are overwhelming.
They remind us that justice must not be reduced to the satisfaction of anger.
And they remind us that mercy can protect a person without declaring every action harmless.
Then Joshua 20:4 gives us one of the most moving details in the entire account.
The person who fled was to stand at the entrance of the city gate and explain his case to the elders.
Imagine that moment.
A terrified man.
A trembling voice.
Dust on his clothing.
Perhaps blood on his hands.
He stands before people who do not know him.
People who have every reason to take the matter seriously.
And he tells them what happened.
The elders were instructed to receive him into the city and provide a place for him to dwell.
He was not supposed to be handed over to the blood avenger merely because someone demanded him.
But neither was his arrival the end of the legal process.
Joshua 20:6 says that he was to remain there until he stood before the congregation for judgment, and, if entitled to refuge, until the death of the high priest serving in those days.
Numbers 35 gives additional details concerning the distinction between murder and unintentional killing, the judgment of the congregation, and the restrictions placed upon the person granted refuge.
This is important.
The city was not an escape from the truth.
It was a protection against unjust retaliation.
The person granted refuge still lived under serious restrictions.
He could not simply return to his former life whenever he wished.
The loss of life remained a grave matter.
Mercy did not erase the consequences of tragedy.
And that is where this ancient story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have spent years wishing that forgiveness meant the past had never happened.
We want the broken trust to disappear.
We want the consequences to vanish.
We want the people we wounded to heal immediately.
We want one apology to undo ten years of damage.
But genuine repentance does not demand that wounded people pretend they were never wounded.
Grace does not make evil good.
Forgiveness does not make every consequence disappear.
And redemption is not the same as rewriting history to make ourselves look innocent.
The Gospel offers something better than denial.
It offers truth, mercy, reconciliation with God, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Sometimes God restores relationships.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt slowly.
Sometimes consequences remain even after forgiveness has been received.
But the presence of consequences does not mean the absence of grace.
Read that again.
The presence of consequences does not mean the absence of grace.
David was forgiven after his terrible sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah, yet his actions brought devastating consequences (2 Samuel 12:13–14).
Peter was restored after denying Jesus, yet he could never claim that his denial had not happened (John 21:15–19).
Paul became an apostle of Christ, yet he never treated his former persecution of the church as something insignificant (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).
Grace did not require these men to lie about their past.
It allowed them to face the truth while being transformed by the mercy of God.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You do not need to invent an innocent version of yourself before you come to Jesus.
You do not need to pretend your words never wounded anyone.
You do not need to deny the choices you made.
You do not need to build a beautiful religious appearance over a conscience that is quietly breaking.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Receive the mercy that only Christ can give.
Because the God who commands justice is also the God who invites sinners to seek His mercy.
But there is another detail in Joshua 20 that is easy to overlook.
God did not establish one city of refuge.
He established six.
Joshua 20:7–8 identifies them.
Kedesh in Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali.
Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim.
Kiriath-arba, also called Hebron, in the hill country of Judah.
And on the eastern side of the Jordan River:
Bezer, in the wilderness plateau associated with Reuben.
Ramoth in Gilead, associated with Gad.
Golan in Bashan, associated with Manasseh.
Three cities west of the Jordan.
Three cities east of the Jordan.
The distribution mattered because the tribes lived on both sides of the river.
The provision of refuge was not confined to one privileged corner of Israel.
God commanded multiple locations so the system of protection could serve the people across the land.
Deuteronomy 19:3 had also instructed Israel to prepare the roads and divide the territory appropriately so that the person who had killed unintentionally could flee.
Picture the mercy in that practical instruction.
God did not merely announce the idea of refuge.
He required His people to make provision for reaching it.
A refuge that exists only in theory is little comfort to a person in danger.
And then Joshua 20:9 reveals something that should arrest our attention.
These cities were appointed not only for the children of Israel but also for the stranger living among them.
The Hebrew text refers to הַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכָם (ha-ger ha-gar betokham), the resident foreigner dwelling among them.
The person was not excluded from this protection simply because he was not an Israelite by birth.
The same legal provision was extended to the resident foreigner who met its conditions.
This was not a declaration that every person was innocent.
It was a declaration that the protection of lawful judgment was not reserved only for those born into Israel.
There is something beautiful about a God who commands His people to remember the vulnerable outsider.
The stranger.
The person without deep family connections.
The one who might otherwise be easier to ignore.
And while the cities of refuge belonged to Israel's specific covenant law, their concern for justice and the protection of human life reflects the character of the God who established them.
Now we must be careful.
Some people read Joshua 20 and turn every detail into a secret prediction about Jesus.
They assign hidden spiritual meanings to every city's name.
They claim each location represents a particular blessing.
They build elaborate systems that sound impressive but cannot be established from the text.
We do not need to do that.
Scripture is already extraordinary without forcing it to say what it never said.
Joshua 20 is first and foremost about real cities, real laws, real human deaths, real grief, and God's provision for people accused of unintentional killing.
But when we read this passage within the whole story of Scripture, we can recognize a profound connection between the need for refuge and the salvation offered in Jesus Christ.
Not because Jesus is merely another city.
Not because the legal provisions are identical.
But because the God who provided refuge under the old covenant has now revealed the fullness of His saving grace in His Son.
Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers as those "who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us." (KJV)
The Greek expression includes καταφυγόντες (kataphygontes), meaning "having fled for refuge."
The word communicates the act of seeking safety.
In Hebrews, that refuge is connected to the certainty of God's promise and the hope secured through Jesus Christ, our great High Priest.
The passage does not explicitly identify Jesus as one of Joshua's cities of refuge.
But its language gives us a powerful biblical connection.
We are people who need a secure hope.
People who cannot save ourselves by moral effort.
People who must depend upon the faithfulness of God.
And Hebrews directs our confidence toward Jesus.
Now consider the difference between the ancient city and the Savior.
The city of refuge was provided for someone who killed unintentionally.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners, including those whose sins were deliberate.
The city offered protection under a particular legal arrangement.
Jesus offers forgiveness and reconciliation with God through His atoning death and resurrection.
The city required the protected person to remain within its boundaries until the appointed release.
Jesus calls His people to abide in Him, not as prisoners confined within stone walls, but as redeemed people who belong to Him.
The city could not cleanse the human heart.
Jesus can.
The city could not conquer death.
Jesus did.
The city could not make a guilty person righteous before God.
Jesus, through His saving work, is the One in whom sinners are justified by grace through faith.
And here is the part that should humble every one of us.
When we stand before the holiness of God, we cannot all claim that our sins were accidents.
Some things we did because we were angry.
Some things we did because we were jealous.
Some things we did because we wanted what God had forbidden.
Some things we said because we knew exactly where the other person's heart was vulnerable.
Some lies were deliberate.
Some betrayals were calculated.
Some compromises were repeated even after conviction had come.
The Bible does not flatter us.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
Not only the person whose scandal became public.
Not only the one who destroyed a marriage.
Not only the person who went to prison.
Not only the addict, the hypocrite, the dishonest leader, or the believer who wandered away.
All.
That includes the person writing these words.
And it includes the person reading them.
We have all fallen short of God's glory.
But the Gospel does not end with Romans 3:23.
Romans 3:24 continues:
"Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "freely" is δωρεὰν (dōrean).
It means freely, as a gift, without being earned by the recipient.
And the word for grace, χάρις (charis), directs our attention to God's undeserved favor.
Do you see what this means?
We cannot purchase forgiveness.
We cannot earn salvation by religious activity.
We cannot donate enough money to erase a single sin.
And that gift cost the Savior more than we can comprehend.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely offer encouraging words to guilty people.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins.
He suffered.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose again.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." (KJV)
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
"For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." (KJV)
The sinless One stood in the place of sinners.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a message about becoming a nicer person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
He did not come to help us decorate our prison.
He came to set captives free.
He did not come to teach us how to hide our shame more effectively.
He came to bring us into the light of His grace.
He did not come to tell us that sin is harmless.
He came to save us from sin's guilt and dominion.
And now I want you to imagine something.
Not a man running toward the gates of ancient Shechem.
Not someone trying to reach Hebron before the blood avenger arrives.
Imagine yourself.
Alone.
Without the audience you usually perform for.
Without the religious language you know how to use.
Without the smile that convinces everyone you are doing fine.
Just you.
Your memories.
Your conscience.
And God.
What is the one thing you wish you could undo?
What conversation still makes your stomach tighten when you remember it?
What sin have you confessed with your lips but continued to protect in your private life?
Whose forgiveness have you refused to seek because your pride keeps telling you that you were justified?
Or perhaps the wound is different.
Perhaps someone sinned against you.
Perhaps you were betrayed by someone who knew Scripture.
Perhaps the person who should have protected you became the reason you struggle to trust.
Perhaps you have watched people use the language of grace to avoid responsibility for the damage they caused.
If that is your story, Joshua 20 offers an important reminder.
God's mercy does not require the abandonment of justice.
You are not commanded to call evil good.
You are not required to expose yourself to continuing abuse.
And forgiveness does not mean that trust must be restored without truth, repentance, wisdom, and appropriate safeguards.
The God who cares for the accused also cares about the person who died and the family left grieving.
The Gospel never asks us to trivialize suffering.
It calls us to bring suffering, sin, judgment, and hope under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And if you are the one who caused the wound, hear this with equal seriousness.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible about being exposed.
Repentance means turning toward God and away from sin.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a change of mind and heart expressed in a changed direction of life.
True repentance does not merely ask, "How can I stop feeling guilty?"
It asks, "Lord, how must I turn from what dishonors You?"
Sometimes repentance means confessing what you have hidden.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that is leading you into sin.
Sometimes it means returning what you stole.
Sometimes it means seeking accountability.
Sometimes it means accepting legal consequences rather than using religious language to escape them.
And sometimes it means admitting that the person you have been blaming for everything is not the only one who needs to change.
That is not easy.
But grace was never meant to become a hiding place for cherished sin.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not simply welcome us.
Grace transforms us.
And here is a truth that might change the way you see your entire past.
Jesus does not need to pretend your scandal never happened in order to write a new chapter of grace.
Look at Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted he would remain faithful.
And then, when fear overwhelmed him, he denied knowing Jesus.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
And Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered His words.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that look?
The Savior he loved.
The promise he had broken.
The sound of his own denial still hanging in the air.
And the unbearable realization that he had failed in the very place where he had been most confident.
But Peter's failure was not the final word over Peter's life.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter did not become a faithful shepherd because his denial was imaginary.
He became a testimony to the restoring grace of the risen Christ.
Not from scandal to pretending.
Not from scandal to religious performance.
Not from scandal to a carefully edited reputation.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by making evil innocent.
Not by denying the suffering of victims.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving repentant sinners, restoring fellowship with God, transforming lives, and giving hope where shame once seemed to have the final word.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this before closing the article.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But you must stop treating the darkness as though it can heal you.
You must stop making peace with what Christ died to redeem you from.
You must stop confusing the ability to quote Scripture with the willingness to obey it.
And you must stop believing that running farther from God will somehow make your soul safer.
The invitation of Jesus is not to run away from Him.
It is to come to Him.
John 6:37 records His promise:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
Think about the tenderness of those words.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
But because the Savior is sufficient.
There is no greater refuge than belonging to the One who died and rose again.
And if your heart is weary, you can pray right now.

"Lord Jesus, I have spent too much of my life running from the truth. You know what I have done. You know what has been done to me. You know the wounds I carry and the sins I have tried to excuse. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Teach me genuine repentance. Give me courage to make what I can right, wisdom to accept what I cannot change, and faith to trust Your mercy. Make me new. Let my life glorify You, not by pretending I have never fallen, but by showing what Your grace can do with a surrendered heart. Amen."
If you prayed that sincerely, do not mistake an emotional moment for the whole journey of discipleship.
Keep turning toward Christ.
Read His Word.
Pray.
Seek fellowship in a faithful local church.
Learn to obey Him.
Where necessary, seek wise pastoral counsel, appropriate professional help, and accountability.
The Christian life is not sustained by one powerful feeling.
It is a life of faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish private details in a comment section.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
You may discover that someone else reading these words has been fighting a similar battle.
And if God has brought you through a season of repentance, restoration, or renewed faith, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Not to glorify the scandal.
But to glorify the Savior.
There is someone on your Facebook friends list who has not told anyone how badly they are struggling.
Someone who still attends church but feels spiritually numb.
Someone who has convinced themselves that God could never welcome them back.
Someone whose shame has become louder than the promises of Scripture.
Not as another religious post to fill a timeline.
But as a simple act of witness.
A reminder that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Invite your family, your friends, those struggling in faith, those searching for answers, and even those who do not yet believe.
The Gospel is not a message reserved for people who already appear spiritually strong.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
And if this ministry has helped you draw nearer to Christ, there is another way you can participate in its mission.

Every article takes time to study, write, examine, and prepare. Every biblical resource shared is an opportunity to encourage someone who may never walk through the doors of a church or approach a pastor with their questions.
But it is important to understand the biblical distinction.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money will purchase divine favor.
But gratitude for the Gospel and a desire to help share its truth.
It is ministry.
It is helping biblical truth reach another weary heart.
Because no financial contribution can replace obedience to Christ.
And no ministry should ever become more important than the Savior it proclaims.
Now return with me, one last time, to Joshua chapter 20.
See the six cities.
Kedesh.
Shechem.
Hebron.
Bezer.
Ramoth.
Golan.
Six real places established under God's command.
Six cities that testified to the seriousness of human life.
Six places where a person accused of unintentional killing could seek protection while justice was administered.
They were not perfect pictures of the Gospel.
They were not substitutes for the cross.
They belonged to a particular moment in God's covenant dealings with Israel.
Yet they still remind us that the Lord is neither indifferent to injustice nor unwilling to provide mercy.
And when we look from Joshua to Jesus, we see something greater than the walls of an ancient city.
We see the Son of God who entered our broken world.
Who was betrayed.
Who was falsely accused.
Who suffered under human injustice.
Who willingly gave His life as the atoning sacrifice for sinners.
Who rose victorious from the grave.
And who now calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
The cities of refuge could shelter a person from an immediate threat under Israel's law.
But only Jesus Christ can reconcile a sinner to God.
Only Jesus can give eternal life.
Only Jesus can make us new.
So stop running from the One who calls you to come home.
Stop allowing shame to tell you that repentance is pointless.
Stop allowing pride to convince you that repentance is unnecessary.
There is truth to face.
There may be wrongs to make right.
There may be consequences to endure.
There may be tears you still need to shed.
But there is also a risen Savior whose grace is greater than anything you could ever earn.
And the invitation still stands.
Come to Christ.
Not because you have nothing to confess.
But because He is mighty to save.
Not because your past is harmless.
But because His redemption is real.
Not because you deserve a second chance.
But because salvation is by grace.
One day, every earthly refuge will fail.
Every human defense will fall silent.
Every reputation will lose its power to protect us.
And what will matter most is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So here is the question I want to leave in your heart.
When your conscience finally stops making excuses, where will you run?
Because somewhere, someone is still running.
Someone is still ashamed.
Someone is still convinced that their story is over.
And perhaps the message you share today will be one of the ways they first hear that Jesus Christ calls sinners to repentance and offers them forgiveness.
The greatest tragedy is not that you once ran in the wrong direction. It is hearing the Savior call you home and choosing to keep running away.
